hook: Her refusal to give up a bus seat sparked the civil rights movement.

pages.x: Rosa McCauley was born in 1913 in Tuskegee, Alabama, and grew up on her grandparents' farm. She remembered her grandfather sitting up at night with a shotgun while the Ku Klux Klan rode by. White children rode a bus to school; Black children walked.
In 1932 she married Raymond Parks, a barber who fought for civil rights. In 1943 she became secretary of the Montgomery branch of the NAACP, and looked into attacks on Black women.

On 1 December 1955, riding home from her job as a seamstress, she refused the driver's order to give up her seat to a white passenger, and was arrested. She said later that she was not tired from work, only tired of giving in.
Others had refused before her, among them a 15-year-old girl, Claudette Colvin, nine months earlier. Leaders chose to fight Parks's case because she was so calm and so widely respected.

For 381 days the Black people of Montgomery refused to ride the buses, walking or sharing cars, led by a young pastor, Martin Luther King Jr. In 1956 the Supreme Court ruled that segregated buses were against the Constitution.
She lost her job and got death threats, and in 1957 moved to Detroit. There she worked for more than 20 years for a congressman, John Conyers.
She received the Presidential Medal of Freedom and the Congressional Gold Medal. When she died in 2005, she became the first woman to lie in honour in the Capitol in Washington.
Her quiet refusal sparked the Montgomery bus boycott and the civil rights movement. She is called the mother of the civil rights movement.
pts: Refused to give up her bus seat in 1955
Called the mother of the civil rights movement
